title: WHY DID JESUS BEGIN WITH JOHN THE BAPTIST?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS BEGIN WITH JOHN THE BAPTIST?
Before Jesus publicly proclaimed the Kingdom, God sent a strange man into the wilderness—and if you understand why, you may never hear the Gospel the same way again.
There is something almost unsettling about the way the Gospel begins.
If you were writing the story of the Son of God entering public ministry, where would you begin?
With the Messiah walking dramatically into Jerusalem while thousands fall at His feet?
That would make sense to us.
But that is not where Mark begins.
“The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God…”

And almost immediately, before Jesus begins preaching, before the disciples leave their nets, before demons scream His identity, before lepers are cleansed, before storms become still, before the cross darkens Jerusalem and before an empty tomb changes human history…
A man standing in the wilderness.
No attempt to make himself impressive.
And that detail matters more than many Christians realize.
Because John the Baptist was not merely the eccentric preacher who happened to appear shortly before Jesus.
John was part of the announcement that the King had arrived.
“Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me.”
Centuries later, Jesus Himself identifies John with this promised messenger when He says in Matthew 11:10:
“For this is he, of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee.”
That means John was not an accidental opening act.
Before the Messiah was publicly revealed, the road had to be prepared.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because God still prepares hearts before He confronts them with the glory of Christ.
John stood between expectation and fulfillment.
Between the old age and the dawning announcement of the Kingdom.
“Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” — Matthew 3:2
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε—metanoeite—from μετανοέω, metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one’s mind, turning in a radically different direction of thought and life. In the biblical proclamation, repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is not crying during worship and returning to the same rebellion on Monday.
It is not being embarrassed because someone discovered what you were doing.
It is not promising God that you will behave better because you are terrified of consequences.
Biblical repentance turns away from sin and toward God.
And suddenly the strange wilderness preacher begins making sense.
Why did the story of Jesus’ public arrival begin with a preacher crying out for repentance?
Because humanity’s greatest problem was never lack of inspiration.
We did not merely need encouragement.
We did not merely need better habits.
We did not merely need another teacher telling us how to climb toward God.
We needed God to come down and rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
And before people could understand the beauty of the Lamb, they needed to understand why a Lamb was necessary.
John was preparing them for Jesus.
That is not a meaningless geographical detail.
“The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.” — Isaiah 40:3
The Gospel writers deliberately connect John with this prophecy.
And look carefully at what Isaiah says is being prepared.
This is one of the breathtaking realities surrounding John’s ministry.
The Gospel is not merely introducing another prophet.
The promised Lord is coming to His people.
When religious leaders ask who he is, John refuses identities that do not belong to him.
He does not try to steal Christ’s spotlight.
He does not build his ministry around making people obsessed with John.
“I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord…” — John 1:23
John knew that a voice exists for the message it carries.
The messenger was never supposed to become more important than the One being announced.
And there is a lesson here that cuts deeply into modern Christianity.
Somewhere along the way, it becomes incredibly easy to want Jesus to increase our importance instead of wanting our lives to increase His glory.
We can serve Jesus and secretly want applause.
Preach Jesus and secretly count reactions.
Sing about Jesus and secretly crave recognition.
Write about Jesus and secretly hunger to become important.
Give to Jesus and secretly want everyone to notice.
Even ministry can become another hiding place for pride.
When Jesus begins attracting more people, John's disciples become concerned.
John… everybody is going to Him.
Do you know how easily insecurity could have entered that moment?
And the crowd began moving away from John.
Imagine watching the thing you spent years building suddenly become smaller because Someone greater appeared.
Many of us would call that failure.
His answer contains one of the most beautiful sentences ever spoken by a servant of God.
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
Ekeinon dei auxanein, eme de elattousthai.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” — John 3:30
This is how it has to be.
And perhaps this is where the article stops being about John the Baptist.
Perhaps now it becomes about you.
Because there is something inside every fallen human heart that desperately wants to be the center of the story.
We want God to bless our plans.
Answer our prayers according to our preferred ending.
And sometimes we unconsciously reduce Jesus to a supporting character in a story starring us.
He was never the main character.
Because if you have to be the center, you have to carry the weight of being the center.
You have to maintain the image.
Pretend you are stronger than you are.
But the Gospel says you can finally stop pretending.
John points toward Jesus and cries:
“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” — John 1:29
The destination of John's entire ministry.
John’s ministry begins with repentance because repentance clears away the illusion that we can rescue ourselves.
And then John points toward the only One who can.
Because the Bible's story had been moving toward sacrifice long before John stood beside the Jordan.
Humanity had rebelled against its Creator.
No amount of religious cosmetics could remove guilt.
Sacrifice runs through the Old Testament, pointing beyond itself toward something greater.
“Behold the One who will make all your dreams come true.”
A Lamb is headed toward sacrifice.
John was pointing toward a cross before many people understood there would be one.
And eventually the innocent Christ would be rejected.
Not because Rome accidentally defeated Him.
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” — John 10:18
At the cross, the scandal becomes almost unbearable.
The righteous One stands where sinners belong.
And the guilty are offered mercy.
We spend our lives trying to prove that good people deserve good things.
The Gospel announces something far more shocking:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we finally conquered every addiction.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how costly forgiveness really is.
Grace is free to the sinner because the price was borne by Christ.
And perhaps you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
Something you have learned to disguise.
But you know how tired you are.
Maybe they see your Bible posts.
But they do not see your private war.
Maybe your family thinks you are okay.
Your church thinks you are okay.
Your friends think you are okay.
Your social media certainly makes it look like you are okay.
But when the room becomes quiet…
The version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever meets.
“If people really knew me, would they still love me?”
There is an even more frightening question.
Every night you promised it would be the last time.
Every prayer you prayed while knowing you intended to return to the same sin.
Not because your sin is small.
Because repentance is the doorway through which we stop defending the disease and run toward the Physician.
Jesus did not come to decorate your chains.
He did not come merely to improve the old you.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature…” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
This is why John had to come first.
People needed to stop staring at themselves long enough to look at the Lamb.
And maybe that is exactly what needs to happen inside us again.
We have become very skilled at asking Jesus to join our lives.
Have we surrendered our lives to Jesus?
“Jesus, help me accomplish what I want.”
One wants Christ as an assistant.
The other receives Christ as Lord.
One asks God to bless the throne we refuse to leave.
The other gets off the throne.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That sentence may be the cure for more spiritual misery than we realize.
Your need to win every argument can decrease.
Your secret sin must lose its throne.
Your obsession with approval can decrease.
And here is the beautiful paradox.
When Christ becomes greater in your life, you do not become worthless.
You finally discover where your worth comes from.
You were never created to manufacture your own value.
You were created by God and for God.
Your deepest identity is not found in your worst scandal.
Not in what someone did to you.
Not in what you did twenty years ago.
Not in the marriage that collapsed.
Not in the night you wish you could erase.
The Gospel does not pretend those wounds and sins are imaginary.
It announces that Jesus Christ is greater than the ruins.
This is the heartbeat behind the words we repeat at Gospel Warrior:
Not because Jesus edits history and pretends the scandal never happened.
Grace transformed Paul into an apostle of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime remaining to repair his reputation.
He had only a dying confession of faith and a crucified King beside him.
And Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
It does not call darkness light.
It enters darkness and brings people into light.
It does not rename sin as righteousness.
It forgives sinners and begins transforming them.
It does not tell the guilty that guilt is imaginary.
It points to a cross where guilt was answered.
And it does not leave Jesus in the tomb.
The Lamb who was slain rose.
Christianity does not ultimately stand around the grave of a dead religious teacher.
And therefore repentance is not walking toward hopelessness.
It is turning toward a living Savior.
Maybe John the Baptist's voice is reaching you across two thousand years.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ died to free you from.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to return.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
That is why it is grace.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the mud.
Not treating grace as permission to sin, but discovering that grace teaches us to belong to the One who loved us enough to die for us.
Maybe someone reading this has been away from God for years.
But your heart knows the truth.
Tonight, the wilderness voice is calling again.
Prepare the way of the Lord.
Not because John can save you.
Not because Gospel Warrior can save you.
Not because a church can save you.
We will never tell you that supporting a ministry purchases God's favor. Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased. Eternal life is God's gift in Christ.

But if this ministry helps you see Jesus more clearly, understand Scripture more deeply, return to prayer, confront sin honestly, encourage wounded believers, or place biblical truth in front of someone who desperately needs it, then you can help us keep that mission moving.
But because truth worth receiving is truth worth carrying.
Someone may have almost given up on Jesus.
Someone may be sitting in a parked car asking God for one reason not to walk away.
Someone may be ashamed to enter a church.
Someone may be scrolling at 2:13 in the morning after falling into the same sin again.
You may never know which share God uses.
Not merely because you liked it.
Send it privately to someone who needs to know that failure does not have to become the final chapter.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind silence.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person Christ is restoring.
Because there may come a night when the old shame speaks again.
John was never pointing toward your ability to save yourself.
Your share does not earn salvation.
It can carry the message of salvation farther.
Your comment does not prove your faith.
But honest words can break the illusion that everyone else is fighting alone.
Your tag might become someone's invitation back to Scripture.
Your saved post might become the truth you need on your own darkest night.
And your support can help us continue putting Gospel-centered material in front of people who might otherwise never encounter it.
He came to bear witness to the Light.
And when the crowds moved from him toward Jesus, John did not panic.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Maybe that is the prayer we need again.
“Take my life and make it Yours.”
“Lord, let everybody see how strong I am.”
“Let them see how merciful You are.”
Because in the end, John the Baptist's greatness was not that millions would remember John.
His greatness was that he knew exactly where to point.
So if your life feels like wilderness right now…
There is still a voice in the wilderness.
Grace is still greater than the scandal.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories that everyone else thought were already finished.
Because one day your name and mine will disappear from people's timelines.
Our bodies will return to dust.
But the King John announced will still be King.
So let this become the cry of our lives:
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
And perhaps the greatest thing God can do with your story is not make everybody remember your name…
but make it impossible for them to forget His.
